blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The p-value is the probability, calculated assuming H₀ and every other assumption of the statistical model are true, of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The p-value answers the question of §8.1: “how unusual would these data be if H₀ were true?” A small p-value means data like these would be unusual under H₀ and the model. A large p-value means they would not be unusual; it does not show that H₀ is true. The p-value is compared with the pre-chosen α: if p < α, reject H₀.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
For a statistic that is approximately normal under H₀:

  1. z = (estimate − value under H₀)/SE. This counts how many standard errors the estimate lies from the H₀ value.
  2. Two-sided p = P(|Z| ≥ |z|) = 2 × [1 − Φ(|z|)].
  3. p < 0.05 exactly when |z| > 1.96, that is, when |estimate − H₀ value| > 1.96 × SE.
  4. That is the same as saying the H₀ value lies outside estimate ± 1.96 × SE, the 95% CI (recall §7.2). So a 95% CI excludes the H₀ value exactly when the two-sided p < 0.05, provided both use the same SE.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
Urban–rural weights (recall §7.2.3), H₀: difference = 0.

  1. z = (1 − 0)/0.406 = 2.46.
  2. Two-sided p = 2 × [1 − Φ(2.46)] = 2 × 0.0069 = 0.014.
  3. 0.014 < 0.05, so reject H₀. Consistently, the 95% CI 0.20 to 1.80 kg excludes 0.
  4. Reading: if urban and rural children truly had the same mean weight (and the model held), a difference of 1 kg or more in either direction would arise in about 1.4% of such pairs of samples.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
Chapter 7’s prop.test output for the CBHI survey trimmed its test lines (recall §7.2.3). Here they are.

cb <- read.csv("data/cbhi_survey.csv")
tab <- table(cb$maternal_education, cb$cbhi_member)
prop.test(x = tab[c("secondary+", "none"), "1"],
          n = rowSums(tab)[c("secondary+", "none")], correct = FALSE)
2 * pnorm(-1/0.406)             # urban-rural: two-sided p, z = 2.46
    2-sample test for equality of proportions without continuity
    correction
...
X-squared = 25.622, df = 1, p-value = 4.153e-07
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.1628515 0.3584235
...
[1] 0.01377591

H₀ is equal membership in the two education groups (observed: 44.5% vs 18.5%). X-squared is z², so z = √25.622 = 5.06, and p = 4.2 × 10⁻⁷ (§9.1.2, the two-proportion z-test, shows why z² equals this chi-square). The CI (0.163 to 0.358) excludes 0, as the tiny p requires; the test’s SE uses the pooled proportion under H₀ (0.0515) while the CI uses the unpooled SE (0.050), so for proportions the CI–test agreement is close rather than exact. The last line is step 2 of the urban–rural calculation. The §7.2.3 caveat applies to the CBHI p-value too: households are clustered in villages, so this SE is too small and the p-value too small (§15.2, clustered data).

blocks.label: Common Misreading
blocks.html: “p = 0.014 means there is a 1.4% probability that H₀ is true” or “a 1.4% probability that the result is due to chance”. Both are wrong. The p-value is calculated assuming H₀ and chance alone; it cannot also be the probability of those assumptions (ASA, 2016, principle 2; Greenland et al., 2016).

points.html: What the p-value is not. It is not the probability that H₀ is true, nor that the data arose by chance alone. It does not measure the size or importance of an effect. A result should not be judged only by whether p crosses a threshold (ASA, 2016, principles 2, 3 and 5).

It tests the whole model. A small p can arise because H₀ is false, or because another assumption failed: non-random sampling, ignored clustering, or selection of the analysis for its small p (Greenland et al., 2016).

Significance is not importance. With a large n, a trivial difference gives a tiny p, because the SE shrinks with √n (recall §6.7). Always report the effect estimate with its confidence interval; the p-value alone says nothing about size or direction.

p-values are continuous. A smaller p does indicate greater incompatibility of the data with H₀ under the model, but p = 0.04 and p = 0.06 are nearly the same evidence, not two different realities. Report the exact p (e.g. p = 0.014), not “p < 0.05”; an inequality is reasonable only for very small values such as p < 0.001 (Greenland et al., 2016).

Multiplicity. Each test at α = 0.05 has a 5% Type I error rate. Run k independent tests on true null hypotheses and the chance of at least one false positive, the family-wise error rate, is 1 − (1 − α)ᵏ. (Each test avoids a false positive with probability 0.95; by the multiplication rule for independent events, recall §5.2.2, all k do so with probability 0.95ᵏ; subtract from 1 by the complement rule, §5.2.3.) For k = 5 it is 1 − 0.95⁵ = 0.226; for k = 10, 0.401; for k = 20, 0.642. Twenty subgroup tests of a useless drug will “find” something about two times in three. The simplest remedy, Bonferroni, tests each at α/k (0.01 for k = 5); §9.5.3 (post-hoc tests) treats Bonferroni, Holm and others. ICH E9 asks trialists to consider adjusting significance levels “to control the overall type I error” whenever more than one test is used (ICH, 1998).
